what_it_does: Huawei's Ascend chip is a purpose-built AI accelerator — a processor designed specifically for AI workloads rather than general-purpose computing. Unlike a GPU where much of the memory management is handled automatically, Ascend requires programmers to manually schedule data movement and synchronize its internal pipeline stages, making it hard to know why a given piece of AI software is slow and what to fix. Existing 'roofline' analysis (a standard technique that draws a ceiling showing the maximum possible speed given either compute capacity or memory bandwidth, whichever runs out first) works well for simpler chips but becomes cluttered and inaccurate when applied to Ascend's multi-component internal structure. This paper builds a component-by-component version of the roofline, with a separate performance ceiling drawn for each internal unit (compute engine, memory buses, data pipeline stages), so engineers can immediately see which component is the bottleneck. It then pairs that diagnosis with a structured set of optimization recipes derived from real case studies on Ascend hardware.
